title: What worker training does the FSMA Produce Safety Rule require on farms?
description: 21 CFR 112.21 to 112.30: annual farm worker training, required topics, harvest training, the supervisor course and records under the Produce Safety Rule.
shortAnswer: Subpart C of the FDA Produce Safety Rule, 21 CFR 112.21 to 112.30, requires covered farms to train everyone who handles covered produce or food contact surfaces, and their supervisors, on hiring and at least once a year, in food hygiene, health and personal hygiene, and the standards relevant to their job. At least one supervisor must complete training equivalent to an FDA recognized curriculum, and the farm must record the date, topics and people trained.
keyTakeaways: 112.21(a) requires training on hiring and periodically thereafter, at least once annually, for all personnel who handle covered produce or food contact surfaces, or supervise them.
112.22(a) sets three core topics: principles of food hygiene and food safety, health and personal hygiene including recognizing symptoms, and the FDA standards relevant to the person's job.
112.22(b) adds harvest specific topics, and 112.22(c) requires at least one supervisor or responsible party to complete training equivalent to an FDA recognized standardized curriculum.
112.30(b) requires training records with the date, topics covered and persons trained, and 112.164 requires records to be kept for at least 2 years.
Farms averaging $25,000 or less in annual produce sales over the previous three years, adjusted for inflation, are not covered.
jurisdiction: United States (federal): Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA); 21 CFR part 112, Standards for the Growing, Harvesting, Packing, and Holding of Produce for Human Consumption
appliesTo: Covered farms: farms and farm mixed type facilities averaging more than $25,000 in annual produce sales over the previous three years, adjusted for inflation
All personnel who handle covered produce or food contact surfaces, including temporary, part time, seasonal and contracted workers
Supervisors and the farm's responsible party

sections.heading: Which farms and workers are covered?

blocks.text: A farm is covered if it averaged more than $25,000 in annual produce sales over the previous three years on a rolling basis, adjusted for inflation from a 2011 baseline, under [21 CFR 112.4](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/112.4). Farms at or below that level are not covered, and some farms that would otherwise be covered qualify for an exemption under 112.5.

Within a covered farm, the training rules apply to all personnel who handle covered produce or food contact surfaces, or who supervise those activities. The text of [112.21](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/112.21) expressly includes temporary, part time, seasonal and contracted personnel, which is the population most likely to be missed when training is tracked through payroll.

[FDA](https://www.fda.gov/food/food-safety-modernization-act-fsma/fsma-final-rule-produce-safety) set staggered compliance dates for most non sprout produce: January 26, 2018 for farms averaging over $500,000 in produce sales, January 28, 2019 for small businesses ($250,000 to $500,000), and January 27, 2020 for very small businesses ($25,000 to $250,000). All have passed, so as at November 2026 every covered farm should be training to the rule.

sections.heading: How often must farm workers be trained?

blocks.text: On hiring and at least once a year after that. 112.21(a) sets the annual minimum, and 112.21(d) requires training to be repeated as necessary when observations or information indicate personnel are not meeting the standards.

blocks.title: Primary text: 21 CFR 112.21(a) and (c)
blocks.text: "All personnel... must receive adequate training, as appropriate to the person's duties, upon hiring, and periodically thereafter, at least once annually." ... "Training must be conducted in a manner that is easily understood by personnel being trained."

The "easily understood" requirement in 112.21(c) has practical consequences for farms with seasonal crews: language, literacy and delivery format all bear on whether training meets the rule. 112.21(b) separately requires each person to have the combination of education, training and experience needed to perform assigned duties in a way that ensures compliance.

sections.heading: What topics must produce safety training cover?

blocks.text: Every covered worker must be trained on three core topics, and harvest workers on three more. [21 CFR 112.22](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/112.22) sets them out.

blocks.caption: Required training topics under 21 CFR 112.22 (as at November 2026)
head: Paragraph

rows: Principles of food hygiene and food safety
Importance of health and personal hygiene for all personnel and visitors, including recognizing symptoms of a health condition reasonably likely to result in contamination

Recognizing covered produce that must not be harvested, including produce that may be contaminated
Inspecting harvest containers and equipment to ensure they function properly and are clean and maintained
Correcting problems with harvest containers or equipment, or reporting them to the supervisor

blocks.text: The health topic links training to subpart D. Under 112.31, personnel must be instructed to notify a supervisor or responsible party if they have, or may have, an applicable health condition, and 112.32 sets hygienic practices such as thorough handwashing with soap and running water. Training is where those instructions are given and evidenced.

sections.heading: What training does a farm supervisor need?

blocks.text: At least one supervisor or responsible party for the farm must have completed food safety training at least equivalent to a standardized curriculum recognized as adequate by FDA, under 112.22(c). FDA names the Produce Safety Alliance (PSA) among the partners it worked with to develop training.

112.23 also requires the farm to assign or identify personnel to supervise, or otherwise be responsible for, its operations to ensure compliance with part 112. Taken together, a farm should be able to name who is responsible and show that at least one such person completed the recognized course or an equivalent.

sections.heading: What training records must a covered farm keep?

blocks.text: A covered farm must keep records documenting required training, including the date, topics covered and the person or persons trained, under [112.30(b)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/112.30), kept for at least 2 years past creation under [112.164](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/112.164). blocks.text: Because seasonal workers often return each year, the annual clock should run per person from their last training, not from the start of the season. See [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) and [how to make elearning accessible](/guides/how-to-make-elearning-accessible) for delivery that meets the easily understood test.

sections.heading: How does this rule relate to other FSMA training rules?

blocks.text: The Produce Safety Rule governs farms; food facilities that process or pack under 21 CFR part 117 follow the [preventive controls qualified individual](/regulations/fsma-preventive-controls-qualified-individual-training) rules and the 117.4 worker training requirement instead. Retail food establishments are governed by state adoptions of the [FDA Food Code](/regulations/fda-food-code-certified-food-protection-manager). A farm mixed type facility can face both part 112 and part 117 for different activities.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry can map the six 112.22 topics to short, assessable outcomes per role, so a farm can show that each seasonal worker was trained on the topics their job requires and that the record captures date, topics and person as 112.30 demands. See [operational procedure programs](/programs/operational-procedures).

faqs.q: Do seasonal and contract farm workers need Produce Safety Rule training?
faqs.a: Yes. 21 CFR 112.21 covers all personnel, including temporary, part time, seasonal and contracted personnel, who handle covered produce or food contact surfaces or supervise those activities. They need training on hiring and at least once annually.

faqs.q: Does every farm worker need the Produce Safety Alliance course?
faqs.a: No. 112.22(c) requires at least one supervisor or responsible party for the farm to complete training equivalent to an FDA recognized standardized curriculum. Other workers need the topic based training in 112.22(a) and, for harvest crews, 112.22(b), which the farm can deliver itself.

faqs.q: What must a Produce Safety Rule training record show?
faqs.a: 112.30(b) requires records documenting required training that include the date of training, the topics covered and the persons trained. Under 112.164, those records must be kept for at least 2 years past the date they were created.

faqs.q: Is a small farm exempt from the Produce Safety Rule?
faqs.a: Farms with an average annual value of produce sold of $25,000 or less over the previous three years, adjusted for inflation, are not covered. Some larger farms may qualify for an exemption under 112.5, which FDA can withdraw under subpart R, so the farm's sales profile should be checked against the rule each year.
